title: Estimate or interpret the slope of the line of best fit
subtitle: Two-variable data: Models and scatterplots · 13 official questions

sections.heading: Where this sits for you
body: **13 of the official questions in Two-variable data: Models and scatterplots are this one** — 1 Easy, 9 Medium, 3 Hard.
It is top-heavy: most versions are Hard, so it only earns study time once your target actually requires that tier.

sections.heading: How to spot it
body: You are looking at this pattern when:
- You see a scatterplot with a drawn line, and the question asks which value is 'closest to the slope', or which sentence is the 'best interpretation of the slope in this context'.

- The choices are either four numbers that often include a positive/negative pair and a value near the y-intercept, or four sentences of the form 'y is predicted to increase by __ for every __ increase in x'.

sections.heading: The method
body: - 1) Check the sign first: if the line falls from left to right, cross out every positive choice.
- 2) Find two points far apart where the line crosses gridlines cleanly, then compute rise over run using the axis scales, not the number of grid squares.
- 3) For interpretation choices, say it as 'y changes by slope per 1 unit of x', using the axis labels to decide which variable goes where.

sections.heading: Where Desmos fits
body: Type your two estimated points into a table and fit y1~mx1+b to get the slope without mental arithmetic.
Usually the sign check plus rough rise over run is faster.

sections.heading: What it is built to catch
body: You pick the choice that equals the y-intercept, flip the sign, or count grid squares when the x and y axes use different scales.
In context questions, you swap the variables, so the sentence says x changes per y instead of y per x.

sections.heading: You are losing these
body: Before you choose, say out loud what the question is asking for — not what you solved for.
You pick the choice that equals the y-intercept, flip the sign, or count grid squares when the x and y axes use different scales.
In context questions, you swap the variables, so the sentence says x changes per y instead of y per x.
